correctness.rationale: With circumradius one, the polygon inradius is \(r=\cos(\pi/n)\) and the equal-area disk radius \(s=\sqrt{\sin(2\pi/n)/(2\pi/n)}\) satisfies \(r<s<1\). For any translated disk center \(x\), rotate the intersection \(P_n\cap(x+B_s)\) through the polygon symmetry group. The Minkowski average of the rotated intersections lies in \(P_n\cap B_s\): convexity keeps the polygon component inside \(P_n\), while the rotated centers average to zero and the averaged disk offsets remain in \(B_s\). Brunn--Minkowski therefore shows the centered disk maximizes overlap. Since \(s<1\), the disk portions beyond adjacent polygon sides do not overlap before the vertices, so the symmetric-difference area is twice \(n\) identical circular caps. The cap formula gives the exact expression. Standard Taylor expansion gives the stated \(n^{-2}\) coefficient and, combined with \(P(S_n)=2\sqrt{n\tan(\pi/n)}\) for unit area, the ratio constant. The package verifier independently integrates the centered intersection and numerically checks the asymptotics; independent evaluations reproduced the finite values and limiting coefficient.

value.rationale: Fraenkel asymmetry is a canonical quantitative-isoperimetric invariant, and regular polygons are a standard calibration family already used in the literature. An exact formula for every \(n\), a proof of the optimizing disk center, and the exact calibration constant convert a previously order-level/asymptotic benchmark into a complete geometric profile.
residual_risks: The contribution is specialized to one highly symmetric family.

final_claim: For every regular Euclidean \(n\)-gon \(P_n\), \(n\ge3\), the equal-area disk centered at the polygon center minimizes the Fraenkel symmetric difference, and with \(t=\pi/n\), \(q_n=\sqrt{\sin(2t)/(2t)}\), and \(\beta_n=\arccos(\cos t/q_n)\), \[\mathcal A_F(P_n)=\frac{2n}{\pi}\bigl(\beta_n-\sin\beta_n\cos\beta_n\bigr).\] Consequently \(\mathcal A_F(P_n)=4\pi^2/(9\sqrt3)n^{-2}+O(n^{-4})\), and the regular-polygon perimeter/Fraenkel asymptotic proportionality constant is \(3\sqrt{3\pi}/4\).
limitations: Only filled regular Euclidean polygons and equal-area Euclidean comparison disks are covered.
The result does not classify all centers that could tie the optimum for more general polygons.
